newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan opposition enters 10th year, faces split.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan opposition enters 10th year, faces split.

text.p: Taiwan's pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party celebrated its tenth anniversary on Saturday, hailing the opposition's achievements in pushing the island toward democracy from authoritarianism.
"Nobody dared to predict what would happen to the Democratic Progressive Party when it was established 10 years ago," party chairman Hsu Hsin-liang said in a speech for the anniversary.

The Democratic Progressive Party, formed in 1986 but legal only after Taiwan lifted martial law in 1987, openly advocates Taiwan independence and is now the island's second biggest political party next to the ruling Nationalist Party.
"No one can deny that if there was no Democratic Progressive Party, there would be no democratic politics in Taiwan," he said.
Many of Taiwan's democratic reforms, including the historic direct presidential elections, were promoted by the party.

However, a rift in the island's pro-independence movement has deepened as a group of activists have decided to form the Taiwan Independence Party on December 12, accusing the biggest opposition of failing to actively promote independence.
"This is not a happy ceremony because we are facing an unprecedented split in the opposition force," former party chairman Shih Ming-teh said at the anniversary.

After recent election results showed that most Taiwanese preferred a status-quo instead of independence or reunification the party softened its stance to say that independence would only be declared if supported in a referendum.
"We should not resort to split hastily," state-funded Central News Agency quoted Shih as saying.
Taiwan, which calls itself the Republic of China, and China have been separated since the end of a civil war in 1949. Both sides say they want reunification, but under different terms.
China threatens to recover the island by force if it goes for independence.
Taiwan maintains an official policy of anti-independence, but says it is an "independent political entity" like the government in Beijing.
